The derivative of a function measures its instantaneous rate of change at a point—the slope of the tangent line to the curve. It is defined as the limit of the secant-line slope: f prime of x equals the limit as h approaches zero of f of x plus h minus f of x, all over h. The derivative is the workhorse of calculus, with applications spanning physics, where velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity; optimization, where you find maxima and minima; and approximation. Computing derivatives by applying rules—power, product, chain, and quotient—is a core calculus skill. By providing a precise way to calculate how a changing quantity varies in real time, differentiation forms the mathematical basis for classical mechanics and rate laws.

The derivative has several notations. f prime of x, df over dx, and Df of x all mean the same thing. Geometrically, f prime of a is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point x equals a. The limit can exist even if f of a is undefined or different from the limit value.

The power rule states that the derivative of x to the n equals n times x to the n minus one. The product rule says that the derivative of fg equals f prime g plus f g prime. The quotient rule gives you the derivative of f over g: f prime g minus fg prime, all over g squared. The chain rule applies to composite functions: the derivative of f composed with g at x equals f prime of g of x times g prime of x.

The first derivative test tells you about the function's behavior: if f prime of x is greater than zero, the function is increasing; if f prime of x is less than zero, it is decreasing. Critical points, where f prime of x equals zero or is undefined, are candidates for local extrema. The second derivative, f double prime of x, measures concavity: when f double prime is greater than zero, the function is concave up; when f double prime is less than zero, it is concave down. L'Hôpital's rule provides a way to evaluate limits that give you indeterminate forms like zero over zero or infinity over infinity: compute the limit of the derivatives instead.

The derivative is the bridge between algebra and calculus. It translates the static question "what is the value at this point?" into the dynamic one "how fast is it changing?" This shift unlocks optimization, curve-sketching, and modeling rates of change in nature. Physics is built entirely on derivatives. Quiz-bowl questions range from basic rule application to interpreting derivatives to applying them to real-world models. The derivative is also the gateway to differential equations.
